fullPassage: Today's mission required a spacewalk, one of the riskiest tasks on the ISS. Scott, my colleague, and I went to an airlock, a room connected to the outside of the station, put on our spacesuits, and floated gently into space. The large blue dome of Earth hovered overhead, looking like it was ready to come crashing down upon us. Forcing myself to focus on the task, I secured the hook of my safety cable to a ring just outside the airlock. We moved along the handrail to the edge of the station. The dark void in front of us seemed endless. Despite the safety cable, panic rose in me. The task seemed to take forever, but I finally managed to install the battery bases. When I turned my head, the bright blue Earth was still there. In the middle of darkness, its beauty was beyond description.

questions.passage: Now I'm getting better at ⓐ remembering where I am when I first wake up, but I'm still often confused about how my body ⓑ is positioned. In the dark and without gravity, my inner ear just takes a random guess as to my position, and sometimes I wake up ⓒ convincing that I'm upside down. Of course, it's actually my brain ⓓ readjusting to an environment where height and weight ⓔ lose their meaning.

det.analysis: 원문: sometimes I wake up convincing that I'm upside down

This protects the planet from the orbital debris that would otherwise rain down on it. After pushing our spaceship away from the station, we eased our way into the upper layers of the atmosphere ⓒ starting our descent. We felt gravity ⓓ begin to return.

questions.passage: Today's mission required a spacewalk, one of the ① <u>riskiest</u> tasks on the ISS. We had to install the bases for some newly developed solar batteries on the outside of the station. Scott, my colleague, and I went to an airlock, put on our spacesuits, and floated ② <u>gently</u> into space. We moved along the handrail to the edge of the station. The dark void in front of us seemed ③ <u>limited</u>. Despite the safety cable, panic ④ <u>rose</u> in me. I thought, "If my hand misses the handrail, I will fall into the void." The task seemed to take forever, but I finally managed to install the battery bases. When I turned my head, the bright blue Earth was still there. In the middle of darkness, its beauty was beyond ⑤ <u>description</u>.

questions.passage: Now I'm getting better at remembering where I am when I first wake up, but I'm still often confused about how my body is positioned. In the dark and without gravity, my inner ear just takes a random guess as to my position, and sometimes I wake up convinced that I'm upside down. Of course, it's actually my brain readjusting to an environment where height and weight lose their meaning. I can use any wall equally as if each were a floor. Everything has zero weight. This enables me not only to fly but also to lift huge objects with one finger as if I were a superhero. Unfortunately, zero gravity also makes astronauts lose muscle and bone density really fast. That's why I exercise for 150 minutes a day as my colleagues do.
questions.stem: 위 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 무중력 환경에서 내이(inner ear)가 위치를 임의로 추측하고, 뇌가 높이와 무게의 의미가 사라진 환경에 재적응하며, 벽을 바닥처럼 사용하고 물체를 한 손가락으로 들 수 있지만, 근육과 골밀도 손실이라는 부작용이 있어 매일 150분 운동한다는 내용입니다.

❌ ① 우주 비행사의 훈련 과정과 선발 기준
✅ ② 무중력 환경이 인체에 미치는 영향과 적응
❌ ③ 우주 정거장의 구조와 설계 원리
❌ ④ 우주에서의 효율적인 시간 관리 방법
❌ ⑤ 우주 비행사의 식생활과 영양 관리

questions.passage: As big as a football field, it is composed of many different sections, such as experiment modules, habitation modules, solar battery panels, and robotic arms. It is a completely unique structure assembled by spacewalkers flying around Earth at 28,000 kilometers per hour in a vacuum in extremes of temperature. It is the result of work by 15 different nations over about two decades. The work was carried out by thousands of people speaking different languages and using different engineering methods and standards. Many astronauts believe that it will stand forever as proof that when humans work together, we can do anything from going to Mars to solving our problems here on Earth.
questions.stem: 위 글이 시사하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 인간이 함께 협력하면 화성에 가는 것부터 지구의 문제를 해결하는 것까지 무엇이든 할 수 있다. → 15개국, 수천 명의 사람들이 서로 다른 언어와 공학 방식으로 협력하여 ISS를 완성한 사례가 국제 협력의 가능성을 보여줍니다.
det.analysis: 원문: when humans work together, we can do anything from going to Mars to solving our problems here on Earth

questions.passage: The station orbits Earth once every 90 minutes, and the sun rises and sets every 45 minutes. However, our schedules are set to Greenwich Mean Time on Earth. My day starts around 6:00 a.m. in my personal space, which is about the size of a phone booth. Still in my sleeping bag, I click through new emails and brush my teeth. I swallow the toothpaste with a sip of water from a bag with a straw. There's no good way to spit in space because everything floats. Every minute of an astronaut's day is planned by the Earth team. My favorite experiment is growing basil from seeds as I film its growth every day.
questions.stem: 위 글의 내용과 일치하는 것은?

det.korean: 나의 하루는 전화 부스 크기 정도인 나의 개인 공간에서 오전 6시경에 시작된다.
det.analysis: 원문: My day starts around 6:00 a.m. in my personal space, which is about the size of a phone booth.
det.tip: 일치 유형 — 지문을 꼼꼼히 읽고 정답을 찾으세요.

우주 비행사가 직접 하루 일정을 계획한다.

questions.passage: After pushing our spaceship away from the station, we eased our way into the upper layers of the atmosphere to start our descent. We felt gravity begin to return. My watch felt a lot heavier on my wrist, and breathing got harder. The capsule heated up, and orange and purple flaming pieces flew by the window, which was scorched black. We were falling faster than the speed of sound. Once we got inside the atmosphere about eight kilometers above the planet, a parachute caught us with a sudden halt and dragged and swung our capsule wildly through the sky until we hit the ground.

det.analysis: 원문: a parachute caught us with a sudden halt and dragged and swung our capsule wildly through the sky until we hit the ground.
